We need a standardized graphic for our project management tool.

treemap.description: Part-to-whole as nested rectangles whose areas show share of the total, laid out by the squarified treemap algorithm (d3-hierarchy treemapSquarify). By default up to four categories: each category is one block and its items are rectangles inside it, with the category name and total in a pill. With an optional per-item path (1 to 3 group names, top down) the chart nests by that path instead, up to three levels of group boxes with a header showing the group name and total, so a folder tree or a cost breakdown reads like a disk-usage map. Each rectangle carries its name and value where the drawn width and height can hold them; in a narrower container or a thin cell the label is hidden (the hover title and the hidden table keep it). A hidden table gives item, category (or path), value and share. Motion-ready: every moving value reads --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1) through a per-item --k, so a motion_timeline track on p builds it item by item and the standalone render is the finished picture; reduced motion shows the end state.

items.description: array (required, 4 to 12) of {category (max 20), name (max 24), value (number above 0), path? (array of 1 to 3 strings, max 20 each, the item's ancestor groups from the top down)}. Without any path at most four categories are drawn; items with a value of 0 or less are dropped. When any item has a usable path the chart nests by path and category is ignored for items that have one; an item without a path goes into a group named by its category, or Other. The item cap is 12 unless max_items is given.

max_items.description: integer (optional, 12 to 60, default 12). Lifts the item cap; items beyond it are not drawn and a note says how many. Any other value keeps 12.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The treemap contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

treemap.x-routing-text: Rectangles sized by value, grouped into up to four categories, or nested up to three levels deep by a path per item (a folder tree, a spend breakdown). Good for a quick sense of share; exact numbers are in a table. Not for precise comparison, and not for more than 12 items.
x-intent-phrases: Show where cloud spend goes by category.
I need a treemap of storage by team.
Visualise the share of each item within its group.
Show what is using my disk space, folder by folder.

histogram.description: The distribution of a list of numbers: bars of counts per bin on a counted y axis, with the bin edges on the x axis. The bins and the rounded axis come from d3-array bin() with the Sturges rule, computed on the server, so there is no script. A hidden table gives each bin from, to and count. Motion-ready: every moving value reads --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1) through a per-item --k, so a motion_timeline track on p grows the bars one after another and the standalone render is the finished picture; reduced motion shows the end state.

values.description: array (required, 5 to 2000) of numbers. Entries that are not finite numbers (text, null, true or false, NaN, Infinity) or whose size is above 1e12 are skipped and counted in a note; with fewer than 5 numbers left a note replaces the chart. Only the first 2000 entries are read.

bins.description: integer (optional, 3 to 40). The number of bins to aim for. Default is the Sturges rule, ceil(log2(n)) + 1. d3 rounds the bin edges to 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten, so the number drawn can differ a little from the number asked for.

x_label.description: string (optional, max 40). Names the values on the x axis.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the x label and to the edge values in the hidden table.

bin_size.description: number (optional, above 0). Explicit bins of this width instead of the Sturges rule; at most 200 bins are drawn, with a note. The last bin ends at bin_end, so it can be narrower than the rest. Draws one series (no overlay or stack as in Plotly). Bins are start + k * size, include their lower edge and exclude the upper, except the last. Values outside the bins are not counted and a note says how many. Not understood values are ignored with a note.

bin_start.description: number (optional). The first bin edge; default the smallest value rounded down to a multiple of the bin size.

bin_end.description: number (optional, above bin_start). The last bin edge; default one bin past the largest value.

norm.description: string (optional, "percent", "probability", "density" or "probability density"). Normalises count or sum. Percent and probability of the total, density per unit of width, probability density per unit of width of the total. Default counts.

cumulative.description: boolean (optional, default false). Only true switches it on; draws the running total over the bins (count or sum only).

func.description: string (optional, "count", "sum", "avg", "min" or "max", default "count"). What a bin shows; all but count need `weights` (without them it counts, with a note). An empty bin shows nothing for avg, min and max.

weights.description: array (optional, same order as values) of numbers, one per value; a value or weight that is not a finite number skips the pair.

layout.description: string (optional, "bars" or "ridge", default "bars"). "ridge" draws one ridge per entry of `series` on shared bins, to compare distributions; `values` is then not read. Any other value draws bars.

series.description: array (optional, read only when layout is "ridge", 1 to 8) of {label (string, max 30, default "Series n"), values (array, 5 to 2000, of numbers, filtered like `values`)}. The shared bins come from d3 bin() of all the series pooled (`bins` applies); each ridge's height is its share of that series' values per bin, so series of different sizes compare. A series with fewer than 5 usable numbers is left out with a note; series beyond the first 8 are noted and not drawn.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The histogram contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

histogram.x-routing-text: Shows how a list of raw numbers is spread out, such as response times, order values or scores. Give the numbers, not the counts; the bins are computed. Not for comparing categories (use a bar chart) or for showing a trend over time.
x-intent-phrases: Show the distribution of these response times.
I need a histogram of order values.
How are these exam scores spread out?
Compare the distributions of wait times before, during and after the change.

box_plot.description: Compares groups of numbers as box plots on one shared horizontal axis: per group a box from the lower to the upper quartile, a line at the median, whiskers to the furthest numbers within 1.5 times the box length, and dots for the outliers beyond. The quartiles come from d3-array quantileSorted and the axis from d3 nice() and ticks(), computed on the server, so there is no script. A hidden table gives each group's count, minimum, quartiles, median, maximum and outlier count. Motion-ready: each group fades in through --k from --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1); the standalone render is the finished picture and reduced motion shows the end state.

groups.description: array (required, 1 to 12) of {label (string, max 30, default "Group n"), values (array, 5 to 2000, of numbers), stats? (object {q1, median, q3, lo?, hi?, min?, max?, mean?, n?}, a precomputed summary drawn instead of values; q1 <= median <= q3)}. Entries that are not finite numbers or whose size is above 1e12 are skipped and counted in a note; a group with fewer than 5 usable numbers, or an entry that is not a group, is left out with a note. Groups beyond the first 12 are noted and not drawn.

x_label.description: string (optional, max 40). Names the values on the axis.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the axis caption and to every value in the label and hidden table.

quartile_method.description: string (optional, "linear", "exclusive" or "inclusive", default "linear" = R-7). Exclusive and inclusive take the median of the lower and upper half (an odd sample's middle value left out, or kept in both). Any option below switches to a static box plot without show_points dots; a note says so if show_points is also given.

show_mean.description: boolean (optional, default false). Only true marks each group's mean with a diamond and adds a Mean column to the table. The mean only; Plotly's boxmean "sd" (mean plus standard deviation) is not drawn.

orientation.description: string (optional, "h" or "v", default "h"). "v" draws vertical boxes on a vertical axis; in a narrow container the group names are replaced by numbers with a key underneath.

notches.description: boolean (optional, default false). Only true draws the median notch, median +/- 1.57 * IQR / sqrt(n), cut at the quartiles. The notch interval is also listed in the table (Notch from, Notch to). (with a note); needs n (the values, or stats.n).

shape.description: string (optional, "box" or "violin", default "box"). "violin" draws a Gaussian kernel density outline (every violin scaled to the same width) with a narrow box inside; it needs values, not stats.

bandwidth.description: number (optional, above 0). The violin kernel bandwidth; default 0.9 * min(sd, IQR / 1.34) * n^-0.2. This is a Silverman-style rule, not the one Plotly uses, so a violin differs slightly from Plotly's. A bandwidth below 1e-6 of the data range is raised to that, with a note.

show_points.description: boolean (optional, default false). Only true switches it on. Draws every usable number of each group as a small dot along its row, at exactly its place on the axis, stacked vertically only as far as needed so no two dots touch (a deterministic dodge beeswarm, no script), behind the box, whiskers and median. Rows are taller. At most 300 dots per chart, shared across the groups in proportion to their sizes and evenly spaced through each group's sorted numbers; a note says so, and the table counts them all. A dot that cannot be placed without touching another stays on the edge of its row; a note counts these.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The box_plot contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

box_plot.x-routing-text: Compares how several groups of raw numbers are spread out, such as response times per region, scores per class or prices per supplier, showing medians, the middle half and outliers side by side. Give the numbers, not the summary statistics. For one distribution's shape use a histogram; for totals per category use a bar chart.
x-intent-phrases: Compare response times across regions with a box plot.
Show the spread of scores for each class.
Which supplier's prices vary the most?

waterfall.description: A running total built step by step, as horizontal bars on one shared axis: each change runs from where the previous step ended (green up, red down) and a total runs from 0 to the running total; dashed connectors join the steps and the signed change is printed at the end of each row, so the direction never rests on colour alone. The axis comes from d3 nice() and ticks(), computed on the server, so there is no script. A hidden table gives each change and the running total. Motion-ready: each step fades in through --k from --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1); the standalone render is the finished picture and reduced motion shows the end state.

steps.description: array (required, 1 to 24) of {label (string, max 30, default "Step n"), value (number), kind (optional, "total" or "delta", default "delta")}. A delta step needs a finite value up to 1e12 in size; a total step without a value shows the running total, and with a value sets the running total to it (a note says when that differs from the steps before it). Other entries are left out with a note; steps beyond the first 24 are noted and not drawn. Any kind other than "total" is a delta.

x_label.description: string (optional, max 40). Names the values on the axis.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the axis caption, the label and every value in the hidden table.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The waterfall contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

waterfall.x-routing-text: Shows how a starting amount is moved up and down by a sequence of changes to an end amount, such as a revenue or budget bridge, a headcount change or a cash flow. Give each change as a signed number and mark totals. For parts of one whole use a treemap or donut; for one value per category use a bar chart.
x-intent-phrases: Build a revenue bridge from last year to this year.
Show what drove the budget from plan to actual as a waterfall.
How did headcount change through hires and leavers?

sunburst.description: Part-to-whole as nested rings: each item is an arc whose angle shows its share of the total, the top-level groups sit in the innermost ring and each level of the optional per-item path (1 to 3 group names, top down) is one ring further out, so a budget, a disk-usage breakdown or a folder tree reads from the inside out. Laid out by d3-hierarchy partition() and drawn with d3-shape arc() paths on the server, so there is no script. With the optional layout "icicle" the same hierarchy is drawn as horizontal bars instead, the top-level groups in the left column and each level one column further right. A group's hue follows its top-level group and each ring out is a lighter shade of it; every arc or bar carries its name, path, value and share in a hover title and in the hidden table (item, path, value, share of total), and the aria label gives the total, the number of groups and the largest group. Labels are drawn only where they fit and are rotated to read outward, never upside down; the centre of the ring shows the total. Motion-ready: every moving value reads --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1) through a per-ring --k, so a motion_timeline track on p builds it ring by ring from the inside out and the standalone render is the finished picture; reduced motion shows the end state.

items.description: array (required, 2 to 40) of {path (optional, array of 0 to 3 strings, max 20 each: the item's ancestor groups from the top down; same shape as the treemap's nested mode), name (max 24, default "Item n"), value (number above 0)}. An item without a usable path is its own arc in the innermost ring. Items with a value of 0 or less, a value that is not a finite number, or that are not an item are dropped and counted in a note; items beyond the first 40 are noted and not drawn. With fewer than 2 usable items a note replaces the chart.

layout.description: "radial" or "icicle" (optional, default "radial"). radial draws concentric rings (a sunburst); icicle draws horizontal bars with the top-level groups on the left. Any other value is drawn as radial.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to every value in the title, the centre, the aria label and the hidden table.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The sunburst contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

sunburst.x-routing-text: Share of a total broken down through up to three levels of groups, as concentric rings (or a horizontal icicle), such as a budget by department and line, disk usage by folder or revenue by region and product. Reads the hierarchy from the inside out. For exact areas side by side use a treemap instead; it is not for a flat list of values, for which use a bar chart.
x-intent-phrases: Show the budget by department and line as a sunburst.
What is using my disk space, folder by folder, as nested rings?
Break revenue down by region, then product, as concentric rings.

chord_diagram.description: Flows between a few entities in both directions as a circle: each group is an arc on the ring (its length is the flow that leaves it) and each ribbon joins two groups, its width at each end showing the flow from that group to the other, so migration between regions, traffic between services or trade between countries reads at a glance. Laid out by d3-chord chord() with sorted subgroups and drawn with d3-shape arc() and d3-chord ribbon() paths on the server, so there is no script. With the optional directed true the same matrix is laid out by chordDirected() and every flow is an arrow (ribbonArrow()) from the sending group to the receiving one, so direction is drawn instead of read from two widths. Each group has its own hue and a ribbon takes the colour of its source group at reduced opacity; every ribbon carries "A to B: value (B to A: value)" (one direction when directed) in a hover title, and the hidden tables list every non-zero flow (from, to, value) and each group's total out and in; the aria label gives the number of groups, the total flow and the largest flow. Group names sit outside the ring, rotated to read outward and never upside down, shortened with an ellipsis where they do not fit and left out where a neighbour is too close (a visible legend always names every group). Motion-ready: every moving value reads --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1) through a per-group --k, so a motion_timeline track on p builds it group by group and the standalone render is the finished picture; reduced motion shows the end state.

groups.description: array (required, 2 to 12) of strings (max 20 each) naming the entities. A name that is not a string or a number is shown as "Group n". Groups beyond the 12th are noted and not drawn, and their rows and columns are dropped. With fewer than 2 groups a note replaces the chart.

matrix.description: array of rows (required): square, one row and one column per group, numbers 0 or more; the cell at row i and column j is the flow from group i to group j (the diagonal is a flow from a group to itself, drawn as a loop). A matrix that is not a list, not square, or whose size does not match groups is replaced by the note "A chord diagram needs a square matrix with one row per group." and what was wrong. A cell that is negative or not a finite number counts as 0 and is counted in a note. If every flow is 0 a note replaces the chart.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to every value in the titles, the aria label and the hidden tables.

directed.description: boolean (optional, default false). false draws chord(): one ribbon joins each pair of groups and its width at each end is the flow from that group (the larger direction is the ribbon's source). true draws chordDirected() with ribbonArrow(): one arrow per non-zero flow, pointing at the receiving group, and a group's arc covers what it sends and what it receives. Any value other than the boolean true is drawn as false.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The chord_diagram contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

chord_diagram.x-routing-text: Flows between a few entities (2 to 12) in both directions, as a ring with a ribbon per pair, such as migration between regions, traffic between services, trade between countries or transfers between teams; set directed to draw each flow as an arrow. For one-way staged flows from sources through stages to outcomes use sankey_flow instead; it is not for more than 12 entities, for a hierarchy (use sunburst or treemap) or for a single list of values (use a bar chart).
x-intent-phrases: Show migration between five regions as a chord diagram.
Which of our services talk to which, and how much traffic goes each way?
Draw the flows between these teams as ribbons around a circle, with arrows for direction.

circle_pack.description: Part-to-whole as packed circles: each item is a circle whose area shows its value, and the optional per-item path (1 to 3 group names, top down) nests the circles inside outlined group circles, so a budget, a skills inventory or a folder tree reads as clusters. Laid out by d3-hierarchy pack() (circle packing: the front-chain placement of packSiblings and the smallest enclosing circle of packEnclose, padding 3) on the server, so there is no script. A group's hue follows its top-level group and a deeper circle is a lighter shade of it; group circles are outlined, leaf circles are filled. Every circle carries its name, path, value and share in a hover title and in the hidden table (item, path, value, share of total), and the aria label gives the total, the number of groups and the largest item. A leaf name (and its value, in a wider container) is drawn inside the circle where it fits, and a group name at the top of its circle where it fits; both are 12 px text gated on the container width. Motion-ready: every moving value reads --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1) through a per-depth --k, so a motion_timeline track on p builds it level by level from the groups inward and the standalone render is the finished picture; reduced motion shows the end state.

items.description: array (required, 2 to 60) of {path (optional, array of 0 to 3 strings, max 20 each: the item's ancestor groups from the top down; same shape as the treemap's nested mode and the sunburst), name (max 24, default "Item n"), value (number above 0)}. An item without a usable path is a circle of its own at the top level. Items with a value of 0 or less, a value that is not a finite number, or that are not an item are dropped and counted in a note; items beyond the first 60 are noted and not drawn. With fewer than 2 usable items a note replaces the chart.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to every value in the title, the aria label, the labels and the hidden table.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The circle_pack contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

circle_pack.x-routing-text: For a sense of grouping and rough size; items as circles packed inside their groups, such as skills by team, files by folder or spend by department and line. For comparing sizes use a treemap or bar chart (circle area is hard to compare); it is not for a flat ranked list, for which use a bar chart, or for share of a total through levels as rings, for which use a sunburst.
x-intent-phrases: Show our team's skills grouped by area as packed circles.
Which folders are taking the space, as a circle packing?
Give me a bubble-cluster view of spend by department and line.

arc_diagram.description: Connections between named things as arcs: the nodes sit on one horizontal line and each link is a semicircle above it joining its two nodes (the d3 gallery "arc diagram"), so a co-authorship list, a module-dependency graph or a who-talks-to-whom table reads as clusters of short arcs and a few long ones. Node positions are even steps along the line (d3-scale scalePoint with padding 0.5) and the arcs are static SVG, so there is no script. Arc thickness shows the link value (1 to 6 px; all links at 2 px when every value is equal). The optional node group sets the dot and the arc colour (an arc takes its source node's) and a legend names every group, but colour is never the only cue: every dot and arc carries its name, group, link count or value in a hover title, and the hidden tables list every node with its group and link count and every link with its two ends and value. The aria label gives the node and link counts and the most connected node. Node names hang below the line rotated 90 degrees; in a narrow container only every second, fourth or eighth name is drawn (the first always) so that none overlaps. Motion-ready: every moving value reads --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1) through a --k, so a motion_timeline track on p draws the arcs and then the nodes and the standalone render is the finished picture; reduced motion shows the end state.

nodes.description: array (required, 2 to 40) of {id (string, max 40: what links refer to), label (string, max 24, default the id), group (optional string, max 20)}. An entry that is not a node, has no id or repeats an earlier id is left out and counted in a note; entries beyond the first 40 are noted and not drawn. With fewer than 2 usable nodes a note replaces the chart.

links.description: array (optional, 0 to 120) of {source (a node id), target (a node id), value (optional number above 0, default 1)}. A link that is not an object, joins a node to itself, names an id that is not a node or has a value that is not a finite number above 0 is dropped and counted in a note; links beyond the first 120 are noted and not drawn. Links are undirected: the arc is always drawn above the line between its two nodes. Parallel links are drawn on top of one another.

order.description: "input" (default), "group" or "degree". input keeps the order of nodes; group sorts by group name and then label (a node without a group first; plain code-unit comparison, ties keep the input order); degree puts the most connected node first (ties keep the input order). Any other value is input.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to every link value in the titles and the hidden table.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The arc_diagram contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

arc_diagram.x-routing-text: Connections between a few dozen named things as arcs over one line, such as who co-wrote with whom, which module imports which or which teams talk to each other; the node order (input, by group or by most connected first) is the story. For flows with amounts use a sankey_flow; for connections between a handful of groups use a chord_diagram; it is not for hierarchies (use a treemap or sunburst) and not for more than 40 nodes.
x-intent-phrases: Show who co-authored with whom as an arc diagram.
Draw which modules import which, as arcs over a line.
Put the nodes on a line and join the connected ones with arcs.

contour_plot.description: Filled contour bands drawn from data: either a grid of values (a temperature, elevation or pressure field) or a cloud of points (the density of delivery locations, incidents or customers). Both use d3-contour: for a grid, marching squares at evenly spaced levels (d3's default count of levels, or the thresholds field); for points, a kernel density estimate (d3 contourDensity: the points are smoothed with the given bandwidth and contoured at up to 20 levels). Bands run from light to dark as the value or density rises, every band is named in a legend as a range of numbers (never colour alone), and a thin outline marks each level. A grid is drawn with column and row numbers on its axes; points use their own x and y with nice axis ticks and are also drawn as faint dots. Static SVG, no script, scaled to its container. The hidden tables give every level with its colour name and, for a grid, the share of cells at or above it, for points the share of points in cells at or above it, then the points themselves (first 200). The aria label gives the mode, the size, the value range and the number of levels. Motion-ready: each band reads --p through a --k so a motion_timeline track on p draws the bands from the lowest level up; the standalone render is the finished picture.

grid.description: object (one of grid or points is required): {width (whole number, 2 to 100), height (whole number, 2 to 100), values (array of width times height numbers, row-major: the first row is the top)}. A value that is not a finite number (or beyond 1e12) is left empty, counted in a note and treated as below every level, as d3 does. A grid whose size is not right gets a note instead of the chart. If points is also given, the grid is drawn and a note says so.

points.description: array (one of grid or points is required, 3 to 2000) of {x, y} numbers. An entry that is not an object with finite numeric x and y is skipped and counted in a note; points beyond the first 2000 are noted and not used; fewer than 3 usable points gets a note instead of the chart. The axes are the data range niced by d3 (a flat range is widened by 1 each side), y up.

thresholds.description: integer (optional, 3 to 20; another number is clamped, a fraction is rounded down). How many levels d3 aims for: ticks at 1, 2 or 5 times a power of ten, so the drawn count can differ. Default: for a grid d3's Sturges count from the number of cells (thresholdSturges); for points 20.

bandwidth.description: number (optional, 5 to 60, default 20; clamped). Points mode only: the smoothing radius of the kernel density, in pixels of the 600 by 400 drawing (it scales with the chart). Larger merges clusters.

x_label.description: string (optional, max 30). Under the plot. A grid defaults to "Column".

y_label.description: string (optional, max 30). Above the plot. A grid defaults to "Row".

value_label.description: string (optional, max 30). Grid mode only, names the values in the legend (default "Value"). Points mode names the density itself.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Grid mode only, appended to the values in the legend, the tables and the aria label.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The contour_plot contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

contour_plot.x-routing-text: A 2D field of values (temperature, elevation, pressure on a grid) or a dense cloud of points (hundreds of delivery locations, incidents, readings) shown as filled contour bands with a range legend. For a few dozen points use a scatter plot; it is not a map (no coordinates, projection or base map, use a geo atom), not a heatmap of categories (a heatmap colours each cell, this draws smoothed regions) and not for more than 100 by 100 grid cells or 2000 points.
x-intent-phrases: Draw contour lines of this temperature grid.
Show where my delivery locations are densest as density contours.
I have a grid of elevation values and want filled contour bands with a legend.

voronoi.description: Nearest-site regions of a set of points: the plot is split into one region per site, each region being every spot that is closer to its site than to any other site (a catchment or service area: which store, depot, sensor or office is nearest). Regions come from a Delaunay triangulation and its Voronoi cells (d3-delaunay, with delaunator and robust-predicates), clipped to the sites' extent plus a margin, with nice axis ticks in the data's own units. Each region is filled with a light colour by group (a legend names every group, never colour alone) or with one light fill and a visible outline when there are no groups; the site is a dot, and its label sits under the dot when the region is wide enough for it (otherwise the label is hidden; the full label is in the region's tooltip and in the table). Static SVG, no script, scaled to its container. The hidden table lists every site with x, y, group, value and its share of the area. The aria label gives the number of sites, the number of groups and the site with the largest region. Motion-ready: each region reads --p through a --k so a motion_timeline track on p fades the regions in one after another; the standalone render is the finished picture.

sites.description: array (required, 3 to 200) of {x, y (numbers, required), label (optional, max 24), group (optional, max 20), value (optional number)}. A site whose position equals an earlier site's is merged into the first, with a note. An entry that is not an object with finite numeric x and y (or beyond 1e12) is left out and counted in a note; entries beyond the first 200 are noted and not used; fewer than 3 sites at different positions gets a note instead of the chart. A label or group that is a number is shown as that number; a list, object or boolean is no text (the site is called "Site 1", "Site 2" ... by its place in the list, and has no group). value is shown in the table and in the region's tooltip only, never drawn.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the values in the table and the tooltips.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The voronoi contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

voronoi.x-routing-text: The nearest-site region of each of a set of points: which store, depot, sensor or office is closest to every spot of an area (catchments, service areas, coverage). It is not a map of real borders or regions (no coordinates, projection or base map; use a choropleth), not for finding clusters or the density of points (use a contour plot or a scatter plot), and distances are straight lines in the x and y units, not travel time along roads. 3 to 200 sites.
x-intent-phrases: Show which of my depots is the nearest to each part of the city.
Draw the service area of each store as nearest-site regions.
Split this area into catchments, one per sensor, by closest distance.

candlestick_chart.description: Price movement as open-high-low-close bars on a date axis, drawn on the server as static HTML with no script. With the default style "candle" each bar is a wick from low to high and a body from open to close; with style "ohlc" it is a stem with a tick to the left for the open and a tick to the right for the close. Direction never rests on colour alone: a bar that closes at or above its open is hollow (candle) or a thin bar (ohlc) in the --positive colour, one that closes lower is filled (candle) or a thick bar (ohlc) in the --negative colour, a legend says so in words, and the hidden table has a Direction column. Bars sit at their real dates (weekend gaps show as gaps), the date axis ticks and labels follow d3-scale scaleUtc and d3-time-format, and the price axis follows d3 nice() and ticks(). An optional volume panel under the price panel repeats the hollow or filled cue. A hidden table gives every value. Motion-ready: each bar fades in through --k from --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1); the standalone render is the finished picture and reduced motion shows the end state.

dates.description: array (required, up to 10000 read) of ISO date strings, read as UTC: "2024-03-05", or with a time "2024-03-05T09:30", "2024-03-05 09:30:15" or "2024-03-05T09:30:15.250Z". Years 1000 to 9000. Any other string, a time zone offset or a non-string leaves that bar out with a note. The bars are drawn in date order.

open.description: array (required) of numbers, one per date, each finite and up to 1e12 in size.

high.description: array (required) of numbers, one per date. Must be at least the open, close and low.

low.description: array (required) of numbers, one per date. Must be at most the open, close and high.

close.description: array (required) of numbers, one per date.

volume.description: array (optional) of numbers of 0 or more, one per date. Adds a volume panel; a bar without a usable volume has no volume bar and a note counts them.

style.description: string (optional, "candle" or "ohlc", default "candle"). Any other value draws candles.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the price values in the aria label and the hidden table.

y_label.description: string (optional, max 40). Names the price axis above the chart.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The candlestick_chart contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

candlestick_chart.x-routing-text: Open, high, low and close values per date, such as a share, fund, currency or commodity price, or any measure with a daily range and an opening and closing value. Give the dates and the four number lists. For one value per date use a line or area chart; for a distribution of values use a box plot; for a running total use a waterfall.
x-intent-phrases: Chart this stock price history as candlesticks.
Show the daily open, high, low and close for the last month with volume.
Draw an OHLC bar chart of the currency rate for each trading day.

parallel_coords.description: Rows of numbers compared across 2 to 8 measures at once: each measure is a vertical axis with its own scale, and each row is one line that crosses every axis at its value, so clusters, trade-offs and outliers across many measures show as bundles of lines. Optionally the lines are coloured by one measure (a light-to-dark ramp from the theme accent, with a legend giving the range). Axis scales come from d3 scaleLinear nice() and ticks() and the lines from d3 line(), computed on the server, so there is no script. The picture is static: the interactive brushing of a Plotly parallel-coordinates chart (dragging on an axis to filter rows) is not available. A hidden table gives every value of every row.

dimensions.description: array (required, 2 to 8) of {label (string, max 24, default "Dimension n"), values (array of numbers), min (number, optional), max (number, optional), reverse (boolean, optional)}. Row i takes values[i] of every dimension, so every dimension lists the rows in the same order. Without min and max the axis runs over the d3 nice() of the values; with both (min below max) the axis is exactly that range and a value outside it is drawn on the edge, with a note (the table keeps the real number). reverse true puts the highest value at the bottom and says so under the label. A row with a missing or non-numeric value (finite, up to 1e12 in size) in any dimension is left out with a note; rows beyond the first 200 and dimensions beyond the first 8 are noted and not drawn. Entries that are not a dimension are left out with a note.

row_labels.description: array (optional) of strings (max 30). Names the rows in the hidden table; default "Row n".

color_by.description: string or integer (optional). The label of a dimension, or its number counting from 0, to colour the lines by. A name that matches no dimension is noted and the lines stay one colour.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The parallel_coords contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

parallel_coords.x-routing-text: Compares rows (cars, models, patients, experiments) across several numeric measures at once as lines over parallel axes, for finding clusters, trade-offs and outliers. Not for two measures (use a scatter plot), not for one measure over time (use a line chart), not for categories with counts (use a bar chart or sankey_flow), and not for more than 200 rows or 8 measures.
x-intent-phrases: Compare these models across accuracy, latency, cost and size at once.
Show how each product ranks on all the measures in a parallel coordinates plot.
Which experiments are good on every metric and which trade one off against another?

ternary_plot.description: Shows what share each of three parts makes up of a whole, one dot per observation, on an equilateral triangle: a point's distance from a corner is how little of that part it has, and the corners are pure A, pure B and pure C. Values are normalised to shares that sum to 100%, gridlines run every 20% on all three axes with their percentages printed on the edges, and an optional dashed line joins the points in the order given. The axis ticks come from d3-scale's linear ticks and the placing is plain trigonometry, computed on the server, so there is no script. A hidden table gives every point's three shares. Static, settled picture; each point fades in through --k from --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1).

a_label.description: string (optional, max 20, default "A"). Names the part at the top corner.

b_label.description: string (optional, max 20, default "B"). Names the part at the bottom left corner.

c_label.description: string (optional, max 20, default "C"). Names the part at the bottom right corner.

points.description: array (required, 1 to 200) of {label (string or number, max 30, default "Point n"), a, b, c (non-negative numbers up to 1e12 in size, not all zero)}. A point whose a, b or c is missing, not a finite number, negative or too large, or that sums to 0, and an entry that is not a point, is left out and counted in a note. Points beyond the first 200 are noted and not drawn.

connect.description: boolean (optional, default false). Only true switches it on. Draws a dashed line through the points in the given order.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The ternary_plot contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

ternary_plot.x-routing-text: Plots observations that are each a mix of exactly three parts, such as soil sand, silt and clay, a vote split between three parties or a budget split three ways. Give three non-negative numbers per point; they are turned into shares. For one share of a whole use a donut or progress bar; for two numbers per point use scatter_trend; for more than three parts use stacked bars or a treemap.
x-intent-phrases: Plot these soil samples by sand, silt and clay on a ternary diagram.
Show how the vote split between three parties moved over the years.
Where does each product sit between price, quality and speed?

quiver.description: A field of arrows on linear axes: each arrow sits on its x, y point and points the way its u (across) and v (up) numbers say, with a length in proportion to the size of the vector. Use it for wind, flow, forces or any vector field. The axes come from d3 nice() and ticks() (d3-scale's linear scale), computed on the server, so there is no script. Arrows are centred on their point, drawn at a fixed size scale so the longest is a set length, and an arrow of length 0 is a dot. A hidden table gives every arrow's x, y, across, up and length. Static, settled picture; each arrow fades in through --k from --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1).

x_label.description: string (optional, max 40, default "x"). Names the horizontal axis.

y_label.description: string (optional, max 40, default "y"). Names the vertical axis.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). The unit of u, v and the length; appended to those values in the table and the label.

arrows.description: array (required, 1 to 200) of {x, y, u, v (finite numbers up to 1e12 in size), label (string or number, max 30, default "Arrow n")}. An entry with a missing or unusable number, or that is not an arrow, is left out and counted in a note. Arrows beyond the first 200 are noted and not drawn.

arrow_scale.description: number (optional, 0.1 to 1, default 1). Shrinks every arrow by this factor; the longest is 120 units of a 1000 unit wide drawing at scale 1. A value that is not a number is ignored.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The quiver contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

quiver.x-routing-text: Draws a vector field, one arrow per point, such as wind speed and direction across a map grid, water flow or the force on each node. Give x, y and the arrow's across (u) and up (v) numbers. It is not for flows between categories (use sankey_flow), for change over time (use a line chart) or for plain points (use scatter_trend). The arrow direction ignores the axis scales (it is the picture angle of (u, v), not scaled by x or y), and arrows are centred on their point, not tail-anchored.
x-intent-phrases: Draw the wind field over this grid as arrows.
Show the direction and strength of the current at each station.
Plot the force vectors on these points.

choropleth_map.description: A map of regions shaded by one number each: world countries, US states or European countries. Give a region_set and a list of {id, value}; the server shades every region in one of 3 to 9 equal-interval classes (steps, default 5), draws a legend of the class ranges and hatches the regions that have no value, so a gap never reads as a low number. Colours come from the theme tokens (sequential accent ramp, or a diverging accent2-to-accent ramp through a neutral middle); Viridis, Turbo and other fixed colour maps are not offered. The outlines are bundled with the catalogue (Natural Earth 1:110m for countries, US Census 1:10m for states): there is no custom GeoJSON, so a region that is not in the set cannot be added. A hidden table lists each region with its code, value and class, largest first, and the regions with no value are listed in a details element. A payload that breaks the rules shows a short note instead of a map.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). Payload contract version.

title.description: string (optional, max 80). Shown above the map and used as its name.

region_set.description: string (required): world-countries (176 countries, Antarctica left out), us-states (the 50 states and DC) or europe-countries (the European subset of world-countries, Russia and Turkey included, framed on the area west of 45 degrees east). Use it to choose which outlines are drawn; the set also decides which ids are valid.

projection.description: string (optional): equal-earth, mercator or albers-usa. Equal Earth keeps areas comparable, so it is the default for world-countries and europe-countries; Mercator suits a close view of Europe but inflates high latitudes; albers-usa (the d3 composite that moves Alaska and Hawaii under the lower 48) is only valid with us-states and is its default. Any other combination, or any other name, shows a note. Use this to change the look, not the data.

values.description: array (required, 1 to 250) of {id (string), value (number)}. id is an ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code for the country sets (for example FRA; Kosovo is XKX) or a 2-letter USPS code for us-states (for example TX; DC is included); case is ignored. value is a finite number of at most 1e15 in size. Entries beyond the 250th are ignored, an unknown id is skipped and named in a note, a repeated id keeps its first value, and an entry without a usable id and number is counted in a note; if nothing matches a region the map is not drawn.

scale.description: object (optional) {kind, scheme?}, the scale contract of chart_legend without the domain (the domain is the data). kind is sequential (default: low to high, one direction) or diverging (a neutral middle, two directions, for values that rise and fall around a centre such as change or difference). scheme is a theme-token ramp name: accent (default) or accent2 for sequential, accent_pair for diverging; any other name falls back to the default. For diverging the centre is 0 when the values cross zero, otherwise the middle of the range. Use diverging only when the centre means something.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the legend ranges and the table values (for example % or USD), with no space before a percent sign.

legend_title.description: string (optional, max 60). A heading for the legend (for example Unemployment rate, %); the map title says what the map is, the legend title says what the colours measure.

steps.description: integer (optional, 3 to 9, default 5). The number of classes. Fewer classes read faster and hide detail; more show detail but neighbouring shades get hard to tell apart. A number outside 3 to 9 is moved to the nearest and named in a note.

frame.description: object (optional) {lon_min, lon_max, lat_min, lat_max}, four finite numbers in degrees: frame the map on a zone (for example a trip) instead of the whole region_set. Longitude is clamped to -180..180 and latitude to -85..85, lat_min must be below lat_max after that, and a span under 1 degree is widened to 1. lon_min above lon_max is a frame across the antimeridian (160 to -150 is a Pacific trip: Fiji, Samoa, Hawaii): the map is drawn with its central meridian at the frame's centre, so outlines, points and routes run on across 180 as one piece; a frame that reaches -180 or 180 is centred the same way, so the land past the seam is drawn. lon_min equal to lon_max is not a frame. A motion_transition between two frames on either side of the seam pans and zooms each keyed region's box (a region drawn in two pieces across the seam travels as one box). A frame that contains no outline of the set is named in a note. A framed map has a sea tint (a mix of theme tokens; left out when the frame reaches past the region set's window, where the set has no land) and rounded corners. The frame is fitted into a fixed 960 x 540 canvas and centred, so two states of one film with different frames have the same box and a motion_transition between them pans and zooms: regions keep their data-key. Outlines outside the frame are drawn and cropped by the viewBox, not dropped. Not used with albers-usa (a fixed composite). A frame that cannot be used is named in a note and the whole map is drawn. Absent: unchanged.

categories.description: array (optional, 1 to 6 names, text up to 40) of category names: switches the map to category mode. Each value is then a category name instead of a number ({id, value: "visited"}); the scale, steps and unit are not used. Each category gets a colour AND a pattern (dots, horizontal stripes, vertical stripes, cross-hatch, backslash stripes, large dots, in list order), so colour is never the only cue; regions with no category are hatched on the surface colour (forward slash) and listed in a details element. The legend lists the categories (data-key class-1 to class-n) and the hidden table lists region, code and category. An entry that names a category not in the list is skipped and counted in a note.

category_colors.description: object (optional) mapping a category name to a theme token name: accent, accent2, text or muted (nothing else, so the map follows the theme in light and dark). A category without an entry, or with another name, takes the default palette by position (accent, accent2, then lighter mixes of them, text and muted) and is named in a note when the name was not a token. Only used with categories.

choropleth_map.x-routing-text: Shade countries (world or Europe) or US states by one number each, with a quantized legend and a text table. Not for points, routes or city-level maps, and not for a map you draw yourself from GeoJSON. For a ranked list of the same numbers use bar_chart.
x-intent-phrases: Show unemployment rate by US state on a map.
Colour the countries of the world by GDP per person.
Map our customer count across Europe.

geo_map.description: Points and lines on a map: dots at latitude and longitude, optionally sized by a number and grouped, and great-circle lines between places, drawn over the same bundled outlines and projections as choropleth_map (world countries, US states or European countries; Equal Earth, Mercator or the US composite). Each group gets its own marker shape as well as its own colour, each line its own dash, so colour is never the only cue. A hidden table lists every point (including any that fall outside the frame, which are noted) and every line. A payload that breaks the rules shows a short note instead of a map.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). Payload contract version.

title.description: string (optional, max 80). Shown above the map and used as its name.

region_set.description: string (optional, default world-countries): world-countries, us-states or europe-countries. Chooses the outlines drawn behind the data and the area the map is framed on; there is no custom GeoJSON and no map tiles.

projection.description: string (optional): equal-earth, mercator or albers-usa. Defaults as in choropleth_map (equal-earth, or albers-usa for us-states); albers-usa is only valid with us-states and moves Alaska and Hawaii under the lower 48. Any other value shows a note.

points.description: array (optional, up to 500) of {lat, lon, id?, label?, value?, group?}. id is text (max 60), the stable key of the point for a build (data-key): without it the key is the label, then the position in the list (p0, p1, ...); a repeated key gets ~2, ~3. lat is -90 to 90 and lon -180 to 180, both finite numbers. label is text (max 40) for the tooltip and the table. value is a finite number that sets the marker size (radius grows with the square root of its place between the smallest and largest value, about 2 to 8 px on a 650 px wide map; a point without a value is the smallest). group is text (max 40); each group gets a marker shape (circle, square, diamond, triangle) and a theme colour in order of first appearance, six groups at most, later groups are shown as Other; the shape and colour pairs of all six groups differ, and points without a group get their own pair and a legend entry Ungrouped (when other points have a group). A point outside the frame (for example Tokyo on a Europe map) is not drawn and is noted. Entries past the 500th are ignored with a note.

lines.description: array (optional, up to 40) of {id?, label?, path: [{lat, lon}, ...]} with 2 to 20 points per path. id is the stable key of the line (as for a point, then the label, then l0, l1, ...). Consecutive points are joined by the great-circle arc between them (d3-geo geoInterpolate, drawn with up to 64 segments each), broken where it crosses the antimeridian so it never streaks across the map. Each line has its own dash (solid, long dash, dotted) and a theme colour.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the values in the legend, tooltips and table.

legend_title.description: string (optional, max 60). A heading for the legend (what the marker size measures).

frame.description: object (optional) {lon_min, lon_max, lat_min, lat_max}: frame the map on a zone (a trip) instead of the whole region_set; the same rules as the frame of choropleth_map (clamped to -180..180 and -85..85, lon_min above lon_max crosses the antimeridian, a span under 1 degree widened, a fixed 960 x 540 canvas, not used with albers-usa, a bad frame is named in a note and the whole map drawn). With a frame every outline carries data-cb "tile" and its region code as data-key, so a motion_transition between two frames moves the whole map as a pan and zoom; points and routes keep their keys and travel with it. Outlines outside the frame are cropped, not dropped; a point outside it is not drawn and is noted. Absent: unchanged.

regions.description: array (optional, up to 250) of {id, category}: shade regions by category (visited, planned, not yet). id is an ISO 3166-1 alpha-3 code (or a USPS code for us-states), category text up to 40. Shaded regions keep their data-key (the code), so they travel in a transition and a region that changes category changes colour. Each category has a colour and a pattern (see categories), listed in the legend, and the hidden table lists region, code and category.

categories.description: array (optional, 1 to 6 names) fixing the category order of regions (so the colours stay the same from one state of a film to the next); without it the categories are the names of regions in first-seen order. Only used with regions.

category_colors.description: object (optional) mapping a category name to accent, accent2, text or muted (theme tokens only); the default palette by position otherwise. Only used with regions.

geo_map.x-routing-text: Place sites, cities, offices or events on a map from latitude and longitude, optionally with routes between them. Not for shading whole countries or states by a number (use choropleth_map), not for a tile map with streets (no map tiles are fetched), and not for a spinning globe (use globe_3d).
x-intent-phrases: Plot our office locations on a world map.
Show shipping routes between these ports.
Mark the cities where we have customers, bigger for more customers.

polar_chart.description: Points and lines placed by angle and distance from a centre: each series gives a radius r and an angle theta for every point, so a compass or wind bearing, a cyclic pattern (hour of day, month) or a radar of scores per category reads as a circular chart. Angles are degrees, or categories (any text) spread evenly around the circle, which draws a radar chart. Up to 6 series are drawn as lines, markers or both, each with its own dash and marker shape so no series depends on colour alone; the optional fill "toself" shades the closed shape of a series. The radial axis starts at 0 (or the lowest negative value) and ends at a round number d3 nice() picks, with circular gridlines at d3 ticks(); an explicit r_range sets it, and a point outside the range is not drawn and is counted in a note. Angles are turned to positions by d3-shape lineRadial() maths and scaled by a d3-scale linear scale, on the server, so there is no script. A large series is thinned to evenly spaced points (the first and last of the points read are kept) with a visible note, the same cap that stands in for Plotly's WebGL scatterpolargl; a series is read up to 5000 points and a longer one says so in a note, so no point is dropped without being counted. The hidden table lists every point with a Status column (drawn, or outside the radial range and not drawn), and the aria label gives the radial range of the drawn points, the categories and each series' extent. Motion-ready: each series fades in through --k from --p (build progress 0 to 1, default 1); the standalone render is the finished picture and reduced motion shows the end state.

series.description: array (required, 1 to 6) of {label (string, max 30, default "Series n"), r (array of numbers, radius of each point), theta (array of numbers in degrees, or strings for categories; same length as r), mode (optional, "lines", "markers" or "lines+markers"; default "lines+markers" up to 20 points, otherwise "lines"), fill (optional, "toself" shades the shape closed from the last point to the first)}. A point needs a finite radius and angle up to 1e12 in size; an entry without a partner or number is skipped and counted in a note; series beyond the first 6 are noted and not drawn. Each series draws at most 2000 divided by the number of series points: a longer one is thinned to evenly spaced points with a note. If any theta is a string, all angles are categories.

categories.description: array (optional, up to 12 strings, max 30 each). Fixes the order of the categories around the circle; categories met in the series after these are added in order of appearance, up to 12 in all (points in later ones are noted and not drawn).

r_range.description: array (optional) of two numbers [low, high], low below high. Sets the radial axis; points outside it are not drawn and are counted in a note. Absent, the axis runs from 0 (or the lowest negative radius) to a round number above the highest.

r_ticks.description: integer (optional, 2 to 8, default 4). About how many circular gridlines the radial axis aims for.

theta_step.description: integer (optional, 30 to 180, default 30). Degrees between the labelled angle spokes of a numeric chart.

direction.description: "clockwise" or "counterclockwise" (optional). Default counterclockwise for numeric angles (as Plotly draws them) and clockwise for categories.

rotation.description: number (optional, -360 to 360). Where angle 0 sits, in degrees counterclockwise from three o'clock. The default follows Plotly: 90 (due north, like a compass) when the direction is clockwise, 0 (due east) when it is counterclockwise; so an explicit "clockwise" starts at the top, which suits wind bearings.

unit.description: string (optional, max 12). Appended to the radial values in the aria label and the hidden table.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The polar_chart contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

polar_chart.x-routing-text: Values placed by an angle and a distance from a centre, such as wind direction against speed, activity by hour of day, a cyclic signal, or scores on several categories compared as a radar. Give each series r and theta (degrees or category names). For a single series of 0 to 100 skill scores use skill_radar; it is not for bars around a circle (radial bars are not offered), for values on straight x and y axes (use scatter_trend) or for part-to-whole (use a pie or sunburst).
x-intent-phrases: Plot wind speed by compass direction on a polar chart.
Compare two products on six criteria as a radar chart.
Show how load varies over the 24 hours of the day around a circle.

histogram2d.description: Counts of x,y points in a grid of 2-D bins (the Plotly histogram2d trace), drawn as a heatmap: d3 bin() is run once on x and once on y, the cell count is the number of points that fall in both bins, and the grid is handed to the heatmap atom, so it has the heatmap colour bar, the cell counts printed inside the cells and a hidden data table. The highest y bin is the top row. Use nbinsx and nbinsy for the number of bins (the real count is the nearest round step, as in d3), or leave them out for the Sturges default. At most 20,000 points are used and at most 40 bins per axis, each with a note.

x.description: array (required, numbers, at least 2 usable pairs with y; up to 20,000 used).

y.description: array (required, numbers, same length as x).

nbinsx.description: integer (optional, 3 to 40, the bin count asked of d3 for x; default Sturges).

nbinsy.description: integer (optional, 3 to 40, the bin count asked of d3 for y; default Sturges).

x_label.description: string (optional, max 40, named in the note under the grid).

y_label.description: string (optional, max 40, named in the note under the grid).

scale.description: string (optional, a heatmap colour scale name such as Blues, Viridis or YlOrRd; default YlGnBu, light for few points and dark for many).

show_values.description: boolean (optional, default true, prints each count in its cell).

version.description: integer (optional, default 1; a higher number draws as version 1 with a muted note).

histogram2d.x-routing-text: Two numeric columns whose joint spread you want to see as counts per cell (density of points, a correlation blob). Not for a grid you already have (use heatmap), not for categories (use heatmap with labels), not for a few points (use scatter_trend), and not for sums or averages of a third value (counts only).
x-intent-phrases: Show where the points are densest as a grid of counts.
I need a 2D histogram of height against weight.
Bin these x and y values into a heatmap of how many fall in each cell.

scatter_matrix.description: A scatter plot matrix (Plotly splom): 2 to 6 numeric dimensions on one grid, every dimension on a shared axis across its row and column, so each cell plots one dimension against another and a pattern between any two shows at a glance. Below the diagonal each cell is a small scatter plot of every complete row (the upper half too with show_upper); the diagonal names the dimension; wide pages also show each dimension's range on the outer edges. Each axis comes from d3 nice() and ticks() on the server, so there is no script. A legend lists every dimension with its range and a hidden table gives every value of every row. Static: no hover or brushing. Motion-ready: each cell fades in through --k from --p (default 1).

dimensions.description: array (required, 2 to 6) of {label (string, max 24, default "Dimension n"), values (array of numbers)}. Row r is the r-th value of every dimension. A row where any dimension has no finite number up to 1e12 in size is left out and counted in a note; an entry that is not a dimension with a list of values is left out with a note; dimensions beyond the first 6 are noted and not drawn. At most 200 complete rows are read; later rows are noted and not drawn. With fewer than 2 dimensions or 2 complete rows a note replaces the chart.

show_upper.description: boolean (optional, default false). Only true also draws the upper half (the same plots with the axes swapped).

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). The scatter_matrix contract the payload was written for. Only version 1 exists; a higher whole number is drawn as version 1 with a note.

scatter_matrix.x-routing-text: Shows how several numeric measures relate to each other at once, such as sepal and petal sizes, or price, area and age of homes, as a grid of small scatter plots. For two measures only use a scatter or trend chart; for many rows on one measure use a histogram; for lines over categories use parallel_coords. It is not for category counts (use parallel_categories).
x-intent-phrases: Plot every measure against every other as a scatter plot matrix.
Show how price, area and age relate to each other in a grid of scatter plots.
Make a splom of these four numeric columns.

motion_transition.description: Morphs one atom into another on the film's progress dial p, joining their elements by data key: two views of the same data (a treemap and a sunburst, a table and an org chart) hand over element by element instead of cross-fading. Each element of the second block that shares a key with the first starts on its partner's box and travels to its own place; with path keys a total starts on the union of its parts (Cloud collects Cloud/VMs and Cloud/Storage) and a part starts on its total; elements only in one block fade. Labels only fade. With reduced motion, on static surfaces or when no timeline sets p, the page shows the second block exactly as it renders alone.

from.description: object (optional). The block shown at p = 0 (any atom). Its elements that carry the build contract (data-cb with data-key) are the start positions; it fades out over the first part of p. Missing: every element of to enters.

to.description: object (required unless patch is given). The block shown at p = 1 (any atom): the page is exactly this block when p is 1, with reduced motion, and on surfaces without script.

patch.description: array (optional) of RFC 6902 JSON Patch operations (add, remove, replace, move, copy, test) applied to a copy of from to make the p = 1 block, in place of to. Use it when the change is a few edits to the same atom (add a person to an org chart, move a card between columns): a copied item grows out of its source, a replaced id continues from the old element, a moved item keeps its key. Needs from; if to is also given, to wins. Up to 500 operations are applied. A patch that fails (bad path, failed test op) shows the from block, with an HTML comment naming the error.

match.description: "path" | "exact" (optional, default path). exact joins identical keys only. path also joins along category paths: a key that is the prefix of others (Cloud, of Cloud/VMs) starts on the union of their boxes, and a key under another (Cloud/VMs, under Cloud) starts on its parent's box.

key_map.description: object (optional, up to 200 pairs). Renames keys of from before the join, from-key to to-key, for two atoms that name the same things differently (a team table keyed by employee id to an org chart keyed by name).

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). Contract version.

motion_transition.x-routing-text: Animate a hand-over from one chart or list to another showing the same data (treemap to sunburst, table to org chart), elements moving by their data key, driven by a motion_timeline p track.
x-intent-phrases: Morph the treemap into a sunburst of the same budget.
Collapse the breakdown into its totals as the film plays.

motion_map3d.description: A tilted 3D city map built from CSS alone (perspective and a rotated plane: no WebGL, no map tiles, no fetch). Blocks stand on a ground plane as three-faced boxes, either a seeded generated city, explicit blocks, or generated district clusters (cities). Outlines of real-world countries or states can be drawn directly on the ground plane under the blocks and route. As p runs 0 to 1 the camera descends and tilts in (p 0 to 0.3), then one or more legs draw on from station to station (p 0.3 to 0.92, optionally bending in arcs and pausing at stations with dwell times) with each station going from idle to active as a leg reaches it and then to its own state (idle, active, done, warn or error), payload chips can travel along the legs, and an optional clock chip counts in clock time, seconds or milliseconds. Station pins and labels sit on their own layer above the city, so blocks never cover them. Made for journeys through a system as much as through a city: a request trace, an agent's tool call and its reply, a deploy pipeline, an incident. At p = 1 every leg is fully drawn, the stations are in their final states and the clock shows its end value.

seed.description: integer (optional). 0 to 9999, default 7. Seeds the generated city when no blocks are given: the same seed always makes the same city. Generated blocks leave the streets under the route and the stations clear, and are lower close to them, so the route is never hidden.

blocks.description: array (optional, up to 200) of {x, y, w, h, height}: x, y, w, h in percent of the map (0 to 100, w and h at least 1) and height the box height (0 to 40, default 6). When given and non-empty they replace the generated city and are drawn exactly as written, so keep your own blocks off the route. More than 200 draw the first 200 with a visible note.

ground.description: object (optional) {set, window, highlight, fill, accent}. Real map outlines drawn directly on the city plane under blocks and routes. set: "world-countries", "europe-countries", or "us-states". window: [lon0, lon1, lat0, lat1] bounding box in degrees (lon -180..180, lat -85..85 with lon0 < lon1 and lat0 < lat1). highlight: array (up to 24) of region id strings. fill and accent: "#rrggbb" colours (defaults #2a3342 and #3a4a63). Example: ground: {set: "europe-countries", window: [-10, 30, 35, 60], highlight: ["FRA", "DEU"]}. Maximum 400 regions and 6000 points; when ground is valid without blocks or cities, the full-plane generated city is omitted.

cities.description: array (optional, up to 8) of {x, y, w, h, count, seed, height}. Clusters of small buildings generated inside rectangular districts (0 to 100 percent map coords). count: 1 to 24 (default 4); height: 1 to 40 (default 8); seed: optional integer (defaults to atom seed + city index). Example: cities: [{x: 20, y: 30, w: 25, h: 25, count: 9}]. Omits the full-plane random city.

arc.description: number 0 to 0.6 or boolean (optional, true = 0.25). Bends route leg segments into quadratic bezier curves bulging outward to the left of travel direction (back legs bend opposite). Example: arc: 0.2 curves all legs gently.

stations.description: array (optional, up to 24) of {id, x, y, lon, lat, label, state, dwell}: id letters, digits and underscore, starting with a letter, max 24 (else s1, s2 by position; a repeated id is left out with a note), x and y in percent of the map (0 to 100, default 50). When a valid ground is active, lon and lat (numbers) can be given instead of x/y and are projected via Web Mercator. dwell: 0 to 0.3, portion of the p dial the route holds at this station before resuming. label max 24 characters (default the id) and state idle, active, done, warn or error (default idle). The state is the settled one: a station on a leg is idle until a leg arrives, active while it is there, then its own state. warn draws an amber pin with "!" and error a red pin with "×", so colour is never the only cue; the text alternative names every state. A station off every leg simply shows its state. Without stations the map shows a note.

route.description: array (optional, up to 32) of station ids in order. Each pair draws one straight or arched segment on the ground. An id that is not a station is skipped with a note, and an id repeated straight after itself is ignored. Ignored when legs has at least one valid leg.

clock.description: object (optional) {from, to, unit}. unit "hhmm" (default; anything else unknown also means hhmm): from and to as HH:MM, 24-hour, a to earlier than from runs through midnight. unit "s" or "ms": from and to are whole non-negative numbers (fractions are floored; s up to 86400, ms up to 3600000) and to must not be below from; the chip reads like 480 ms or 1560 s. The chip at the top left counts over p 0.3 to 0.92. Both values must be valid or no chip is drawn.

tilt.description: number (optional). Final camera tilt in degrees, 0 (straight down) to 75, default 55. The camera starts straight down and tilts in over p 0 to 0.3.

camera.description: object (optional) {from, to, keys, follow, track}. from and to: zoom of the map at p 0 and at the end of the descent, 0.3 to 3, defaults 0.55 and 1. keys: array (up to 8) of {at, turn, tilt, zoom}, poses the camera passes through over the whole film instead of the default descent: at is p (0 to 1, each later than the one before), turn the rotation of the map in degrees (-180 to 180, default 22), tilt 0 to 75, zoom 0.3 to 3; a missing value keeps the previous key's; held before the first key and after the last; bad keys are left out with a note. follow: integer 1 to 6 (used only without keys): after the descent the camera turns to a new angle each time the route arrives at every follow-th station, and swings round and closes in on the last destination (a little closer at each stop). track: 0 to 1, how firmly the camera pans to keep the head of the route (where it is drawing now) at the centre, so the view rides along the journey; default 0.6 with follow, otherwise 0 (no pan). Station pins and labels keep their size and keep facing the viewer at every angle.

color.description: "#rrggbb" (optional). Route and active-station colour. Default the stage accent.

legs.description: array (optional, up to 4) of {route, color, back}: several legs drawn one after another, replacing route when at least one is valid. route is station ids as in route (a leg needs two known stations, else it is left out with a note); color "#rrggbb" (default the atom colour); back true reverses the leg, for a reply going back along the path, and draws it in its own lane beside the outbound leg. The drawing window is shared by all legs in proportion to their length. Segment keys run over all legs (from-to, a repeat gets -2, -3).

messages.description: array (optional, up to 12) of {leg, text, at, back}: a payload chip that travels along a leg while it is drawn. leg is an index into the drawn legs (default 0); text max 24 characters; at the p (0 to 1) when it sets off (default the leg's own start); back true sends it from the leg's end to its start. A chip is visible only while it travels, so the settled frame shows none; the text alternative lists every message with its start and end station. Bad entries are left out with a note.

version.description: integer (optional, default 1). 1 and 2 draw the same; a whole number above 2 draws as version 2 with a muted note.

motion_map3d.x-routing-text: A tilted three-dimensional city map scene: camera dropping in over blocks or real map outlines, route legs drawing from stop to stop with the stations lighting up as they arrive, payload chips travelling along the legs, stations ending done, warn or error, and a clock chip counting clock time, seconds or milliseconds. Use it for a journey through a system told spatially: a request trace through gateway, services and database with latency, an AI agent calling an MCP tool and the reply coming back, a CI/CD pipeline with a failed or warning gate, an incident timeline, a data pipeline, failover between regions, as well as a delivery or transit tracker. Not a flat schematic of lines (use motion_path, motion_arch or a flow diagram), not map tiles or a real map provider, not a WebGL scene (use motion_shader), not a chart.
x-intent-phrases: A tilted 3D city map where the camera drops in and a delivery route draws from stop to stop.
Show a courier route across city blocks with stations turning active then done and a clock counting up.
Animate a transit route on a 3D map with a time chip.
Animate a request moving through the API gateway, auth service and database with a millisecond latency clock, the database hop failing.
Show an AI agent calling an MCP tool on a 3D map: the request leg goes out, the reply comes back in its own lane, payload chips travel along.
A deploy pipeline as a 3D city route from commit to production with the security scan gate flagged as a warning and a seconds clock.
Replay last night's incident as a route through the services that were hit, ending in error and done states.
Animate an international flight path curving across European countries on a 3D map.
